```{r setup}
#| include: false
# Figures come from scripts/90_report_figs.R (figs/<figure>_<profile>.png + manifest.csv).
# The CONUS ("full") version of a figure is shown when it exists, otherwise the dev one.
figs <- if (file.exists("figs/manifest.csv")) {
  utils::read.csv("figs/manifest.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
} else data.frame(figure = character(), profile = character())

show_fig <- function(name, caption, alt = caption) {
  m <- figs[figs$figure == name, , drop = FALSE]
  pick <- intersect(c("full", "dev"), m$profile)
  pick <- pick[file.exists(sprintf("figs/%s_%s.png", name, pick))]
  if (!length(pick)) {
    cat(sprintf('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Figure pending\n%s\n:::\n\n',
                caption))
    return(invisible())
  }
  r <- m[m$profile == pick[1], ][1, ]
  note <- sprintf("[%s · %s · figure made %s]{.fig-meta}", r$extent, r$years, r$made)
  cat(sprintf('\n![%s %s](figs/%s_%s.png){#fig-%s fig-alt="%s" .column-page-right}\n\n',
              caption, note, name, pick[1], gsub("_", "-", name), alt))
}
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Work in progress
This page tracks an ongoing analysis and is updated as the work moves along. Results
shown here are **preliminary** and some come from a small Arizona test area. They are
here to show the approach and invite feedback, not for operational use. The
[changelog](#changelog) lists what changed and when.
:::

## At a glance

**The question.** Where across the contiguous U.S. do herbaceous fuels (grasses and
forbs) share a common seasonal pattern of green-up, staying green and curing? Regions
like that are the domains we need to build and tune **regional phenology models**
for live fuel moisture, instead of applying one set of thresholds everywhere.

**The approach.** Two independent ways of drawing regions, then compare them:

- **Cut A, climate:** cluster grid cells on climate descriptors built from daily PRISM
  data. These regions are *hypotheses about what drives* fuel phenology.
- **Cut B, satellite curves:** cluster grid cells on the observed seasonal curves of
  greenness and canopy water from MODIS. This is the *response* and the real test of
  Cut A.
- **Ground observations** from the USA National Phenology Network (NPN) and
  iNaturalist provide an independent check, including in places where satellite
  curves and land-cover maps are hardest to interpret.

Where the climate and satellite regions agree, there is a solid basis for regional
models. Where they disagree is where to look for what's missing.

**Status (October 2026).**

| Component | Status |
|---|---|
| Daily PRISM climate, 4 km, CONUS, 2001–2025 | Done |
| Grid, elevation and herbaceous cover layers (Annual NLCD) | Done |
| MODIS greenness and canopy water, CONUS, 2001–2025 | Done (Terra and Aqua merged, smoothed daily curves per year) |
| Cut A, Block 1: seasonal climate features | Done (CONUS, water years 2002–2025) |
| Cut A, Block 2: timing and variability features | Done (CONUS) |
| Cut A, Block 3: GSI sub-indices | Planned (moisture ramp to decide) |
| Cut A clustering: A1 (Block 1) and A2 (Blocks 1 + 2) | First runs done |
| Cut B clustering of satellite curves | First runs done |
| Comparison with satellite curves and ground observations (NPN, live fuel moisture, iNaturalist) | First runs done; choosing the number of regions |

: Pipeline status {.striped}

## Why regions?

The Growing Season Index (GSI; Jolly et al. 2005) in the National Fire Danger Rating
System turns daily minimum temperature, vapor pressure deficit and day length into an
index of plant activity, which is then mapped to live fuel moisture. The same
thresholds are applied everywhere, but herbaceous fuels in a desert grassland watered by
the summer monsoon, a shortgrass prairie, and a California annual grassland respond to
different cues on different calendars.

In discussions with fire managers and planners, the need that came up was **fuel
phenology regionalization**: a data-driven way to find regions with roughly common
green-up, maintenance and curing patterns, so that phenology models can be built and
tuned within each one. We start with **herbaceous fuels** and draw regions **wall to
wall across CONUS**. That way they can be tested anywhere, including in the East where
land-cover maps are challenging, and ground observations anywhere can be used. The
regions can later roll up to the two NFDRS live fuel classes.

## How the analysis is built

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 7
%%{init: {"themeVariables": {"fontSize": "17px"}}}%%
flowchart LR
  P["Daily PRISM 4 km<br/>ppt, tmin, tmax, vpdmax<br/>2001–2025"] --> B1["Block 1<br/>seasonal climate"]
  P --> B2["Block 2<br/>timing and variability"]
  P --> B3["Block 3<br/>GSI sub-indices"]
  B1 --> A["Cut A<br/>climate regions"]
  B2 --> A
  B3 --> A
  M["MODIS NDVI and NDII7<br/>Terra + Aqua, 1 km to 4 km"] --> C["Cut B<br/>seasonal-curve regions"]
  N["NLCD herbaceous cover"] -. "weights and mask" .-> A
  N -. "selects grass-dominated cells" .-> C
  A --> X{"Compare"}
  C --> X
  O["NPN and iNaturalist<br/>phenophase observations"] --> X
  X --> R["Fuel phenology regions<br/>for regional phenology models"]
```

Everything sits on the PRISM 4 km grid (about 480,000 land cells). Features are
computed **for each year and then summarized across years** (median and year-to-year
spread), never from an average-year climate: the GSI of an average year is not the
average GSI.

### Data

| Data set | What it provides | Resolution and period |
|---|---|---|
| PRISM daily (Oregon State University) | Precipitation, min and max temperature, max vapor pressure deficit | 4 km, daily, 2001–2025 |
| MODIS MOD13A2 (Terra) and MYD13A2 (Aqua), Collection 6.1, via NASA AppEEARS | NDVI (greenness); NIR and MIR reflectance for NDII7 (canopy water and curing) | 1 km, 16-day composites, averaged to 4 km; 2001–2025 (Aqua from mid-2002) |
| Annual NLCD Collection 1 (USGS) | Grassland, shrub/scrub, pasture, crop shares per 4 km cell | 30 m land cover for 2001, 2012 and 2024 |
| USA-NPN and iNaturalist | Ground observations of phenophases (green-up, flowering, senescence) | Point observations, CONUS |

: Data sets {.striped}

## Study domain and herbaceous cover

Regions cover all CONUS land. Herbaceous cover from Annual NLCD is used to **describe and
weight** cells, not to define the domain. Two shares are kept: a *core* share
(grassland plus shrub/scrub) and an *open* share that adds pasture and hay, which is the
main herbaceous cover in the East. A **strict mask** (core share at least half of the land
and crops under a quarter) picks out the cells where a MODIS curve is mostly a
herbaceous signal. It is used to select Cut B curves and for sensitivity runs.

```{r fig-domain}
#| results: asis
show_fig("domain",
  "Herbaceous cover on the 4 km grid from Annual NLCD (mean of 2001, 2012 and 2024). The strict mask covers about a third of CONUS land, almost all of it in the West and Great Plains.",
  "Three maps of CONUS: core herbaceous share, open herbaceous share, and the strict herbaceous mask.")
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="true"}
## Why grassland and shrub are combined
In NLCD the split between grassland/herbaceous and shrub/scrub changes abruptly at
some state lines (for example Wyoming/Nebraska, Colorado/Kansas, New Mexico/Texas),
a mapping artifact rather than a real change in vegetation. The analysis therefore only
uses the combined share, never grassland alone.
:::

## Cut A: climate features

The climate features come in three blocks, which are added one at a time so we can see
what each contributes: **A1** = Block 1 + elevation and latitude, **A2** = A1 + Block 2,
**A3** = A2 + Block 3. Keeping the GSI-based features in their own block answers a
practical question: does the GSI formulation add information about where phenology
differs, or do its thresholds steer the regions?

### Block 1: seasonal climate (built)

The year runs from October through September (a *water year*) for temperature,
precipitation and aridity, because cool-season moisture comes before the green-up it
feeds. Freeze dates and growing degree days use the calendar year.

| Feature | Definition |
|---|---|
| Seasonal and annual temperature | Mean of daily (tmin + tmax)/2 for Oct–Dec, Jan–Mar, Apr–Jun, Jul–Sep and the water year; warmest-minus-coolest season range |
| Annual precipitation and seasonal shares | Water-year total and the fraction falling in each season (Jul–Sep isolates the monsoon; Apr–Jun the dry foresummer) |
| Aridity index | Precipitation / potential evapotranspiration (Hargreaves), for the water year and the warm season (Apr–Sep) |
| Freeze dates and freeze-free season | Last spring and first fall day with tmin ≤ 0 °C, and the days between them; ≤ −2.2 °C as a sensitivity check |
| Growing degree days | Base 5 °C (cool-season and general growth) and base 10 °C (warm-season grasses) |

: Block 1 features (21 per year) {.striped}

```{r fig-block1-medians}
#| results: asis
show_fig("block1_medians",
  "Six of the Block 1 features, as the median across years.",
  "Six maps of Block 1 climate features: mean annual temperature, annual precipitation, July to September share of precipitation, aridity index, freeze-free season length, and growing degree days above 10 C.")
```

How a feature varies **from year to year** matters as much as its typical value:
grasses in a place where summer rain is unreliable behave differently from grasses
where it always arrives. Block 1 keeps the spread (interquartile range, IQR) of every
feature alongside its median.

```{r fig-block1-iqr}
#| results: asis
show_fig("block1_iqr",
  "Year-to-year spread of three Block 1 features (interquartile range across years; precipitation as IQR relative to the median).",
  "Three maps of year-to-year variability: annual precipitation, July to September share of precipitation, and freeze-free season length.")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Reading the preliminary maps
- Medians and spreads are across water years 2002–2025.
- Where no freeze occurs, the freeze-free season is set to the full year. Along the
  California coast, south Texas and Florida, years with and without a freeze mix, which
  shows up as a large year-to-year spread in freeze-free season length.
- The aridity index is very skewed (most of the West is well below 1), so it will be
  log- or rank-transformed before clustering.
:::

### Block 2: timing and variability (built)

Herbaceous phenology responds to the **timing and reliability** of moisture and warmth,
not just the averages. Block 2 is computed per year from daily PRISM and summarized as the
median, the year-to-year spread, and coefficients of variation.

| Feature | Definition |
|---|---|
| Warm-season rain onset | First wet day from May 1 that starts a 10-day total of at least 20 mm, with no dry spell of 20 days or more in the following 30 days; no onset by September 30 is recorded as "no onset" (and the share of years with an onset is kept) |
| Rain pulses | Days with at least 5 mm in the warm (Apr–Sep) and cool (Oct–Mar) seasons; 2.5 and 10 mm as sensitivity checks |
| Dry spells | Longest warm-season run of days under 1 mm, and the number of warm-season dry spells of 20 days or more |
| False starts | Growing degree days (base 5 °C) accumulated before the last spring hard freeze (≤ −2.2 °C) |
| Limiting factor | Share of the year that is cold-limited (30-day mean temperature under 5 °C) or moisture-limited (30-day precipitation under half of potential evapotranspiration) |
| Year-to-year variability | Coefficient of variation of annual and warm-season precipitation; standard deviation of Apr–Jun temperature |

: Block 2 features {.striped}

### Block 3: GSI sub-indices (planned)

The daily GSI sub-indices (minimum temperature, vapor pressure deficit, day length and a
moisture ramp), computed per year, give the share of the active season limited by each
factor, and the onset, peak and decline dates of the smoothed index. PRISM has no soil
moisture, so the moisture ramp will use a precipitation-based index or a simple water
balance, and that choice will be treated as a sensitivity test. Vapor pressure deficit is
the least reliable PRISM variable, so A3 will be run with and without it.

## Cut B: satellite seasonal curves

Cut B uses MODIS 16-day composites from both Terra and Aqua at 1 km, averaged to the
4 km grid using only good-quality pixels. The count of valid pixels and the share
flagged as snow are kept for every composite. Two indices describe the season:

- **NDVI** for greenness;
- **NDII7** = (NIR − MIR) / (NIR + MIR) for canopy water content. It drops as grasses
  cure, often separating from NDVI when plants are still green but drying.

```{r fig-cutb-curves}
#| results: asis
show_fig("cutb_curves",
  "16-day NDVI and NDII7 at sample grassland locations, Terra and Aqua.",
  "Time series of NDVI and NDII7 at sample grassland locations, with Terra and Aqua shown as separate lines.")
```

```{r fig-cutb-peak}
#| results: asis
show_fig("cutb_peak",
  "Size of the NDVI seasonal cycle and when it peaks, from one year of Terra composites. Cells with an amplitude under 0.1 have no clear green season.",
  "Two maps: NDVI seasonal amplitude, and the timing of peak NDVI in three seasons.")
```

For each year the two sensors are merged (Terra reads slightly higher than Aqua in
NDII7, so the median difference per cell is split between them), composites with too few
good pixels or too much snow are dropped, and a weighted smoother that follows the upper
envelope of the data (clouds and snow pull values down) gives a curve every 8 days from
October of the previous year through March of the next. From those curves come green-up,
peak, end of season and curing dates, amplitudes, and the median curve across years that
the clustering uses. Cut B is run two ways: on the curves as they are (**level + shape**:
how green and when) and on curves rescaled by their own amplitude (**timing only**).

## First regions and how well they work

Both cuts were clustered with k-means for 4 to 20 regions (Cut A up to 30). Within a block,
features are grouped (for Block 1: temperature, moisture amount, seasonality) and each
group gets equal weight, so the eight temperature features don't outvote the rest. The
number of regions is **not chosen yet**; the comparisons below are what that choice will
rest on. Seven regions is where the A2 climate regions are most stable under resampling;
around 13 the climate regions begin to split the tallgrass prairie from the northern
Midwest and the California annual grasslands from the Mojave.

```{r fig-regions}
#| results: asis
show_fig("regions",
  "First climate (top) and satellite-curve (bottom) regions. Region colours are matched to the first map where regions overlap, so the same colour across maps means mostly the same area. Climate regions are smooth by construction; satellite regions follow land cover and are patchier.",
  "Six maps of CONUS regions: climate A1 with 10 regions, climate A2 with 7 and 13 regions, satellite-curve regions with 7 and 13 regions, and timing-only satellite regions with 13 regions.")
```

### Do climate regions explain the satellite curves?

For each set of regions, the share of the variation in the median satellite curves
(NDVI and NDII7) that lies *between* regions rather than within them. This is scored twice:
on the curves as observed, where how green a place gets dominates, and on the curves
scaled by their own seasonal amplitude, which leaves only **timing** (when green-up, peak
and curing happen), the part that matters most for regional phenology models. The satellite
regions are fitted to these curves, so they show roughly how much any set of that size
can explain. The *location only* baseline divides the map into compact blobs with no
climate information: a useful set of regions has to beat it.

```{r fig-eval-curves}
#| results: asis
show_fig("eval_curves",
  "Share of the satellite-curve variance explained by each set of regions, by number of regions: curves as observed (top) and timing only (bottom). Dashed vertical lines mark 7, 10 and 13 regions.",
  "Four line charts of variance explained versus number of regions, for all cells and for the strict herbaceous mask, one line per set of regions.")
```

### Do the regions separate observed phenology on the ground?

Ground observations come from three sources: USA-NPN observations of grasses (percent
green canopy, giving green-up, curing and cured dates) and other plants (leaf onset and
end), the Globe-LFMC live fuel moisture database (date of the seasonal peak and of the
50 % decline), and iNaturalist flowering records. Each site (one plant type at one place)
is reduced to its median date across years. The score is the adjusted R-squared of those
dates on region: how much of the spread in dates is between regions, with a penalty for
using more regions.

```{r fig-eval-obs}
#| results: asis
show_fig("eval_obs",
  "How well each set of regions separates observed dates (adjusted R-squared of site median dates on region), by number of regions. Bars at 7, 10 and 13 regions show the range over 90 % of block resamples of the sites.",
  "Six line charts of adjusted R-squared versus number of regions for NPN grass green-up, curing and cured dates, live fuel moisture peaks for herbaceous and woody fuels, and iNaturalist flowering onset.")
```

```{r tbl-eval}
#| results: asis
es <- NULL
for (pr in c("full", "dev")) {
  f <- sprintf("figs/eval_summary_%s.csv", pr)
  if (file.exists(f)) { es <- utils::read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE); break }
}
if (!is.null(es)) {
  plab <- c(A1_groups = "Climate A1", A2_groups = "Climate A2", B_raw = "Satellite (level + shape)",
            B_shape = "Satellite (timing only)", geo = "Location only")
  clab <- c(curves_all = "Curves, all cells", curves_herb = "Curves, herb mask",
            timing_all = "Timing, all cells", timing_herb = "Timing, herb mask",
            grass_greenup = "Grass green-up", grass_curing = "Grass curing", grass_cured = "Grass cured",
            lfmc_herb_peak = "LFMC herb peak", lfmc_woody_peak = "LFMC woody peak",
            inat_flower = "iNat flowering")
  es$partition <- ifelse(es$partition %in% names(plab), plab[es$partition], es$partition)
  num <- setdiff(names(es), c("partition", "k"))
  es[num] <- lapply(es[num], function(v) sprintf("%.2f", v))
  names(es) <- c("Regions", "k", ifelse(num %in% names(clab), clab[num], num))
  cat(knitr::kable(es, align = c("l", "r", rep("r", length(num))),
                   caption = "Scores at 7, 10 and 13 regions: share of satellite-curve variance explained, and adjusted R-squared of observed dates on region"),
      sep = "\n")
} else {
  cat('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Table pending\nScores at 7, 10 and 13 regions.\n:::\n\n')
}
```

```{r tbl-eval-diff}
#| results: asis
ed <- NULL
for (pr in c("full", "dev")) {
  f <- sprintf("figs/eval_diff_%s.csv", pr)
  if (file.exists(f)) { ed <- utils::read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE); break }
}
if (!is.null(ed)) {
  ed$cell <- sprintf("%+.2f (%+.2f to %+.2f)", ed$diff, ed$lo, ed$hi)
  w <- stats::reshape(ed[, c("set", "comparison", "k", "cell")], idvar = c("set", "comparison"),
                      timevar = "k", direction = "wide")
  names(w) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(w))
  names(w)[1:2] <- c("Observations", "Comparison")
  names(w)[-(1:2)] <- paste(names(w)[-(1:2)], "regions")
  cat('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true"}\n## How sure are these differences?\n',
      'Differences in adjusted R-squared between two sets of regions, scored on the same resampled sites. ',
      'Sites are resampled in 2-degree blocks, because nearby sites are not independent; the range covers ',
      '90 % of 500 resamples. A range that spans zero means the observations cannot tell the two apart.\n\n', sep = "")
  cat(knitr::kable(w, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "l", rep("r", ncol(w) - 2))), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n:::\n\n")
}
```

## Reading the first comparisons
- **Climate regions capture seasonal timing better than location alone.** On the
  timing-only curves in herbaceous cells, A1 explains 50, 54 and 58 % of the variance at
  7, 10 and 13 regions, against 36, 45 and 47 % for compact blobs of the same number.
- **Adding Block 2 (A2) does not improve the national scores.** A1 and A2 are tied on
  timing (A2: 49, 53, 55 %), and A1 is ahead on the curves as observed in herbaceous
  cells (40 vs 29 % at 7 regions, 53 vs 50 % at 13). Against the ground observations, the
  A2-minus-A1 range spans zero for every data set. Block 2's gains are local: at 13
  regions A2 separates the Kansas and Oklahoma tallgrass prairie from the eastern Corn
  Belt and the California annual grasslands from the Mojave.
- **The level + shape satellite regions mostly sort cells by how green they get.** They
  explain the curves best (they are fitted to them) but separate the ground dates poorly.
- **Where the ground data can judge, climate wins.** Climate regions clearly beat location
  alone for the woody live fuel moisture peak (about +0.12 to +0.21 in adjusted
  R-squared), iNaturalist flowering (+0.05) and grass cured dates at 7 regions (+0.25).
  Grass green-up beats location only at 13 regions. At 10 to 13 regions location alone
  does as well on grass curing and cured dates: with about 150 to 190 grass sites,
  clustered in a few places, the observations cannot judge finer regions.
- **NPN leaf onset and end** for herbaceous and woody plants barely separate by any set of
  regions (adjusted R-squared under 0.07) and are likely too noisy as site medians.
- **Number of regions:** about 13 regions describes herbaceous timing best, but several of
  those regions have fewer than five grass sites and no herbaceous fuel moisture sites,
  so fitting phenology models in every region is not yet possible. About 7 regions, the
  most stable level of A2, is what today's observations can support.
:::

## Clustering and evaluation plan

Methods will be judged by how well the regions work as domains for regional phenology
models, not by clustering scores alone.

- **First runs (Cut A):** k-means as a baseline, Gaussian mixtures (soft membership
  shows transition zones), and Ward hierarchical clustering (nested regions: fine for
  modeling, coarse for operational roll-up). A spatially constrained version tests how
  much is lost by requiring contiguous regions.
- **Cut B:** functional PCA of the seasonal curves, then mixtures on the scores.
- **Linking A and B:** cluster the curves, then predict those regions from the climate
  features with random forests. This gives a wall-to-wall map and shows which climate
  features separate phenology regions.
- **Evaluation:** stability under resampling of years and space; agreement between
  the A1, A2, A3 and Cut B partitions; comparison with EPA ecoregions and operational
  units (Predictive Service Areas, NFDRS climate classes); and whether NPN and
  iNaturalist phenophase dates differ more between regions than within them.

## Decisions so far

| Date | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Oct 2026 | Start with herbaceous fuels; regions are domains for regional phenology models | Most direct need raised by fire managers; herbaceous fuels respond fastest |
| Oct 2026 | Build Cut A from daily PRISM at 4 km; features per year, then summarized | Daily data capture timing and variability; averaging climate first distorts nonlinear indices like GSI |
| Oct 2026 | Herbaceous cover from Annual NLCD (grassland + shrub/scrub; 2001, 2012, 2024) | Consistent national product; combined share avoids the state-line artifact |
| Oct 2026 | Regions are wall to wall across CONUS | Lets NPN and iNaturalist observations anywhere test the regions; cover is an attribute, not the domain |
| Oct 2026 | Cut B from MODIS MOD13A2 + MYD13A2 (1 km, 16-day), averaged to 4 km; NDVI and NDII7 | Available nationally through AppEEARS; two sensors double the sampling; NDII7 tracks curing |
| Oct 2026 | Data period starts in 2001 | First full year of MODIS, so the climate and satellite cuts overlap |
| Oct 2026 | Block 1 definitions: water year, Oct–Dec/Jan–Mar/Apr–Jun/Jul–Sep seasons, GDD base 5 and 10 °C, freeze at 0 °C (−2.2 °C sensitivity), Hargreaves aridity | Seasons isolate the monsoon and the dry foresummer; bases fit cool- and warm-season grasses |
| Oct 2026 | Soils deferred | No quick national water-holding capacity layer; add if the first runs suggest it matters |
| Oct 2026 | Block 2 definitions: rain event ≥ 5 mm (2.5 and 10 mm sensitivity), dry day < 1 mm, warm-season onset rule (10-day total ≥ 20 mm from May 1, no 20-day dry spell in the next 30), hard freeze ≤ −2.2 °C | Event size that wets the root zone of grasses; onset rule screens out false starts |
| Oct 2026 | Feature groups weighted equally within a block (temperature, moisture amount, seasonality) | With one group, temperature features dominated and the Plains moisture gradient was lost |
| Oct 2026 | Working climate regions: A1 at 10 regions, pending the comparison with satellite curves and ground observations | Stable, and separates the main grassland types |

: Analysis decisions {.striped}

## Open questions for the team

- **Study period:** use all of 2001–2025, or a fixed recent window?
- **Number of regions:** a few broad regions (about 7, most stable) or finer ones
  (about 13, which split the tallgrass prairie and the California grasslands)?
- **GSI moisture ramp:** which precipitation or water-balance index to use in Block 3?
- **Ground observations:** which NPN and iNaturalist taxa and phenophases best
  represent herbaceous fuel green-up and curing?
- **Operational use:** how contiguous do regions need to be to be useful to managers?
- **C3/C4 grasses:** is there a suitable national layer of cool- versus warm-season
  grass cover?

Comments on any of these are welcome.
